Substitute every abbreviation separately, without shared subexpressions or loop unrolling. Counting a variable occurrence initially as one gives:

<div class="center">

| Clause                | Nodes | Variable occurrences | Binders |
|:----------------------|------:|---------------------:|--------:|
| Symmetry              |    53 |                   26 |       2 |
| Bottom condition      |   173 |                   68 |       4 |
| Triangle condition    |   240 |                   92 |       4 |
| Order reflection      |   198 |                   72 |       4 |
| Mask and connectivity |   717 |                  281 |      13 |
| Full $Q$              |  1394 |                  542 |      28 |

</div>

The last line adds four conjunction nodes and the outer existential: its binder and the seven-node bound $n^{j^{1+1}}$ contribute nine nodes with the quantifier itself. Renaming the expanded binders consecutively as $v_{100},\ldots,v_{127}$ avoids all capture; the bound of each quantifier is renamed in the preceding environment. Only $v_1,v_2,v_3$ remain free. Every node then costs at most $128$, so $Q$ costs at most $128\cdot1394=178432$. Outside the two numeral assignments, the rest of the program costs $29$: initialization costs $6$, the while and negation nodes cost $2$, increment costs $11$, final output costs $6$, and the four sequencing nodes cost $4$. In particular the following much larger allowance bounds the entire program: <a id="q:program-size"></a>$$\label{q:program-size}
 100(n+1)^3+(2\cdot10^6)^{204}
                      <2^{(M_*+10)^4}=k.$$ The second summand exceeds $178461$. For the strict inequality, $M_*+1\le2^{M_*}$ bounds the first summand by $2^{3M_*+7}$, and $2\cdot10^6<2^{21}$ bounds the second by $2^{4284}$. Since $M_*>10^9$, their sum is less than $2^{3M_*+8}$, which is less than $2^{(M_*+10)^4}$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q-witness-cutoff"></a>
<div id="q:witness-cutoff" class="lemma">

**Lemma 99** (Uniform Busy Beaver witness cutoff). *If $1\le n\le M_*$, $0\le t<2^{n^2}$, and $P(n,t)$ holds, then <a id="q:finite-cutoff"></a>$$\label{q:finite-cutoff}
 \mathcal R(T_{n,t})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
                   (\exists j\in\{1,\ldots,B\})\ Q(n,t,j).$$ In fact every representable such table has a witness of size strictly less than $B$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q-witness-cutoff"><summary>Proof of stmt-q-witness-cutoff</summary>

*Proof.* For a representable table, [q:arithmetic-criterion](#q:arithmetic-criterion) makes the program in [q:search-size](#q:search-size) terminate with a witness size $j$. Its size is less than $k$, so the definition of $B$ gives $j<B$. Conversely, any $j\le B$ satisfying $Q(n,t,j)$ supplies a representation by [q:arithmetic-criterion](#q:arithmetic-criterion). ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q-minimum"></a>
<div id="q:minimum" class="theorem">

**Theorem 18** (Finite description of a minimum example). *The bounded formulas <a href="#q:selection-z" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:selection-z">[q:selection-z]</a>–<a href="#q:minimum-order" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:minimum-order">[q:minimum-order]</a>, with the ordinary unevaluated Busy Beaver constant <a href="#q:BB-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:BB-bound">[q:BB-bound]</a>, specify the full finite order table of a nonrepresentable lattice $L_0$ of minimum cardinality. Its cardinality is the integer $a_0$ in <a href="#q:a0t0" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:a0t0">[q:a0t0]</a>, and $$7<a_0\le M_*.$$ This is a finite order description and a proof of minimum cardinality; it does not supply a numerically evaluated value of that cardinality.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q-minimum"><summary>Proof of stmt-q-minimum</summary>

*Proof.* By [q:witness-cutoff](#q:witness-cutoff), for every index in $\mathcal I$ the bit $z_{n,t}$ is one exactly when the table is a nonrepresentable lattice. By [q:size-ceiling](#q:size-ceiling), some such bit is one. Let $(n_*,t_*)$ be the first index for which it is one. The product in <a href="#q:selection-w" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:selection-w">[q:selection-w]</a> is one at that index; at each later index it contains the zero factor $1-z_{n_*,t_*}$, and at each earlier index the factor $z_{n,t}$ is zero. Hence exactly one $w_{n,t}$ equals one. Formula <a href="#q:a0t0" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:a0t0">[q:a0t0]</a> gives $a_0=n_*$ and $t_0=t_*$, so <a href="#q:minimum-order" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:minimum-order">[q:minimum-order]</a> is precisely this lattice’s full order table. It is nonrepresentable.

Every nonempty lattice of cardinality smaller than $a_0$ has an order table among earlier indices in $\mathcal I$. Its selection bit is zero and its lattice predicate is true, so the cutoff lemma makes it representable. Thus $L_0$ has minimum cardinality among all finite nonrepresentable lattices. The represented range through seven elements in [f:small-lattices](#f:small-lattices) gives $a_0>7$, and its index gives $a_0\le M_*$. Nothing in this argument evaluates $B$: all its uses concern the outputs of the terminating programs in its definition. The result is therefore the claimed finite description with an exhaustive bound, rather than a numerical enumeration. ◻

</details>

The constants and entries above are unambiguous in the standard natural numbers. Their definition supplies no ordinary computable procedure for evaluating the Busy Beaver constant, no evaluated decimal value of $a_0$, and no conventional small diagram of the minimum lattice. Those would be stronger forms of identification than the finite description proved here.

<details id="proof-stmt-q-minimum-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-q-minimum</summary>

*Proof of [m:main](#m:main).* Part <span class="upright">(i)</span> is [f:criterion](#f:criterion); Part <span class="upright">(ii)</span> is [n:undecidable](#n:undecidable). The finite description and its minimum-cardinality property are proved in [q:minimum](#q:minimum). The strict lower bound of seven follows from [f:small-lattices](#f:small-lattices). Part <span class="upright">(iv)</span> is Corollary <a href="#n:interval-undecidable" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n:interval-undecidable">3</a>. ◻

</details>

      "caption": "The two uses of the structural argument. The affine branch gives a negative lattice and a computable size ceiling independently of any hypothetical decider. The weighted branch combines simultaneous arithmetic readings with a separate, weight-independent count; a decider would then bound positive Diophantine solutions. Finite graph witnesses also supply the bounded searches used, with the size ceiling, in the minimum-table specification.",
      "figure_id": "fig:proof-overview",
      "pdf_page": 6,
      "source_evidence": [
        {
          "anchor": "fig:proof-overview",
          "exact_quote": "The two uses of the structural argument.  The affine branch\ngives a negative lattice and a computable size ceiling independently of\nany hypothetical decider.  The weighted branch combines simultaneous\narithmetic readings with a separate, we",
          "source_object": "fig:0001"
        }
      ],
      "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[\n  box/.style={draw,rounded corners=2pt,align=center,text width=4.7cm,\n    inner sep=6pt,font=\\small},\n  arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]},thick},\n  node distance=10mm and 13mm]\n\\node[box,text width=8.2cm] (engine)\n  {Simultaneous pruning in actual simple groups\\\\\n   and the protected-path bound};\n\\node[box] (affine) at (-3.2,-1.7)\n  {Private affine charts:\\\\a nonrepresentable family};\n\\node[box] (marker) at (3.2,-1.7)\n  {Reverse tests and\\\\the forward marker theorem};\n\\node[box,below=of affine] (ceiling)\n  {Effective parameter control:\\\\a computable size ceiling\\\\for one negative lattice};\n\\node[box,below=of marker] (weighted)\n  {Weighted representations:\\\\one cell alignment for\\\\all arithmetic readings};\n\\node[box,below=of ceiling] (graph)\n  {Finite graph witnesses:\\\\affirmative search and\\\\conditional size bounds};\n\\node[box,below=of weighted] (count)\n  {Independent template count:\\\\lattice size bounded by units,\\\\not numerical weights};\n\\node[box,below=of graph] (minimum)\n  {An ordinary Busy Beaver cutoff\\\\and finite selection of a\\\\minimum negative order table};\n\\node[box,below=of count] (undec)\n  {Bounded replacement of\\\\Diophantine solutions:\\\\no representation decider};\n\\draw[arr] (engine.south west) -- (affine.north);\n\\draw[arr] (engine.south east) -- (marker.north);\n\\draw[arr] (affine) -- (ceiling);\n\\draw[arr] (marker) -- (weighted);\n\\draw[arr] (ceiling.west) -- ++(-0.35,0) |- (minimum.west);\n\\draw[arr] (graph) -- (minimum);\n\\draw[arr] (graph.south east) -- (undec.north west);\n\\draw[arr] (count) -- (undec);\n\\draw[arr] (weighted.east) -- ++(0.35,0) |- (undec.east);\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "A flowchart outlining the structural argument with directed arrows connecting rectangular boxes. At the top: \"Simultaneous pruning in actual simple groups and the protected-path bound\". This splits via two arrows into two columns: left box \"Private affine charts: a nonrepresentable family\" and right box \"Reverse tests and the forward marker theorem\". The left box points down to \"Effective parameter control: a computable size ceiling for one negative lattice\", which in turn points down to \"Finite graph witnesses: affirmative search and conditional size bounds\". From this box, two arrows emerge: one pointing down to \"An ordinary Busy Beaver cutoff and finite selection of a minimum negative order table\", and one pointing diagonally down-right to \"Bounded replacement of Diophantine solutions: no representation decider\". The right column proceeds from \"Reverse tests and the forward marker theorem\" down to \"Weighted representations: one cell alignment for all arithmetic readings\", which points down to \"Independent template count: lattice size bounded by units, not numerical weights\", which points diagonally down-left to \"Bounded replacement of Diophantine solutions: no representation decider\"."

      "explanation": "Undecidability strengthens the existence of a finite obstruction: universal representability would give a constant affirmative decider.",

      "source_anchor": "stmt-n-undecidable",
      "source_pm_id": "PM-206.1",
      "source_quote": "There is no algorithm which, given the tables of a finite lattice, decides whether it is isomorphic to the congruence lattice of a finite algebra.
